He had no experience with the internal affairs department, and he was appointed to a professional position, obviously on the basis of a recommendation and liking of the accused, because I know that they were close friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to clear up this question with respect to the regulations and whether things functioned accordingly. But if it didn't, how do you know that it didn't?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a partial answer to that straight away. At a meeting held on the 17th of May, 1999, which was not attended by the Minister of Internal Affairs of Serbia, you tasked the head of the state security department to pass on to the minister what you are saying, as if he was of higher rank than the minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that that head of the state security department was the assistant of that minister, and as the minister was not present, his assistant was present. Isn't it only logical for the assistant who is present, because the minister is not present, to convey to him what happened at the meeting, just as you would pass on to your superior whatever needed to be passed on if he was absent? What is more logical than that? He represents the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of Serbia. He's the assistant minister, a post he was appointed to by the government. And at -- every morning at meetings of the government, each head reports on the activities of his department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm stopping you because this is going well beyond the original question. General, can you answer what's being put by the accused here? Would you wish him to clarify the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recognise the point of the question. Let me say straight away it is not normal for a junior to be told what he should tell a senior. I was there not only because I was in the army. Any conclusions that may have been reached, I would pass on to my immediate subordinate. So we seem to not be hearing one another. The head of the state security is allegedly said to be subordinate to the minister, and the president is asking him to pass it on to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that I did not invite him to the meeting? And do you know, for instance, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait. There was a question. "How do you know that I did not invite him to the meeting?" That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that no general from the MUP was present, nor was the Minister of the Interior, if we're talking about the meeting on the 17th of May. Now, whether after that you passed on this information, I don't know. I assume you did. I just said what you told Rade Markovic, that he should pass on to the minister what was discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you find that that is not logical, that he should brief the minister about everything said at the meeting? You don't find that logical?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, it was not logical for five leading generals to attend the meeting from the army without anyone from at least approximate rank from the MUP, who are familiar with the situation on the ground, to attend that meeting. I find that illogical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you don't know, for instance, but we'll come to that meeting because that came at the end of your testimony, so we'll come to it in due course, but do you happen to know that the minister was supposed to come, and only an hour prior to the meeting he apologised because he had a high temperature and he said, "But Rade's there, and he will inform me about everything," which is quite customary, and there's no drama, no big deal that someone didn't attend the meeting. This was no secret meeting for the Minister of the Interior or for any of you from the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you now. On the contrary, it shouldn't be any secret. But first of all, you didn't tell us why those responsible people from the public security were not present. If he was ill, surely another three generals did not have a temperature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I needed to justify myself to you why someone was not attending a meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question of justification, it's a question of regular politeness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we'll come that meeting. But maybe you'll feel embarrassed when you see some things linked to that meeting, embarrassed on account of the things you said here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are not proper comments. If you've got some questions, you can ask them, not commenting like this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, if we take into consideration the regulations that I've read out to you, the method in which the army functioned, as well as the armed forces of Yugoslavia, tell me, please, was it logical for you to say that the commander of the Territorial Defence of Vojvodina, General Mandaric in those days, was at the command post of General Panic, the commander of the 1st Army? Was that logical?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned this as a positive case; where units of the defence of Vojvodina were active, that their commander should be present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is fully in compliance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we've made that clear. In that context, you said that I said that Serbia was not at war. What's so bad about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course Serbia was not at war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We did support Yugoslavia, and we supported the JNA in its functions, but Serbia was not at war. Or do you consider that Serbia was at war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the remark that Serbia was not at war, and then you go on to say that Serbia supported the JNA, why, then, was there no reaction to the failure of thousands of military reservists to respond to the call-up? I think about 12.000 of them for whom criminal charges were filed because of avoidance to serve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a question that the army should have dealt with and not the bodies of the Republic of Serbia. You know that well.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The army addresses a request to the MUP to find such people and bring them to the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a rather unimportant question regarding your testimony, so we'll move on. There are several things that you mentioned here as some kind of facts. I will follow the order in which you spoke, and probably, according to the concept of Mr. Nice, he goes to some less important things and then the most important things, and he goes back and forth, so it's rather confusing, this order of his, but you say, for instance, speaking about the arming, you say that paramilitary units in Eastern Slavonia had some trophy rifles, automatic Thompson rifles, which you assumed had been taken from the warehouses of the Territorial Defence of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that I knew that such weapons existed within the Territorial Defence of Serbia. I know that for certain. And then I assume that from those depots they were distributed in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you assume that from those depots these weapons were given to Eastern Slavonia. That is your assumption.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some more precise information which I didn't mention, and that is specifically that it came from one particular warehouse of the TO in the environs of Belgrade on the road leading to Valjevo. So from that warehouse, some weapons went to Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned here various persons who took part in the distribution of weapons, certain colonels, certain other officers and so on. And as far as I was able to gather, this did not happen on the basis of instructions from higher-level structures of the JNA who were the owners of these warehouses. But this went according to some friendly connections, people wanting to help somebody without any specific orders coming along the chain of command, "Deliver those weapons. Arm those people." Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's make this quite clear: Then you took as an example a request which you yourself called a megalomaniac, and it was shown here as an exhibit where somewhere in Bosnia the leadership is addressed and asked that the army provide for the needs of the police helicopters, armoured vehicles, anti-aircraft guns, weapons, communications devices, and you yourself said it was a megalomaniac as a request addressed to the army. That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this happened in different time periods. These -- this individual distribution of weapons, a couple of pieces, maybe more, this occurred sometime in the first half of 1991. And as for these requests that you are referring to now, came in 1992. So that is in the period when the forces of the TO and the MUP in Krajina were preparing to constitute themselves as units which would later come under international control. So these are two different time periods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But we're talking here about Bosnia, not Croatia at all.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't say Bosnia or Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said it was Bosnia, and you showed a document relating to Bosnia. The document was shown here listing a request needed for -- materials needed in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain. Those were units that were also asking for weapons because they were close to Krajina. This is the centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is the following, General: Was that request complied with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what, then, does such a request prove, a request addressed by a local leadership to the army which the army did not comply with? What does that prove, then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't prove anything. I said it was a megalomaniac request that was not met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't say that it was not met. You just said it was megalomaniac and so on. But it was not met?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. We are going to pause between question and answer because of the interpreters. You said that in the autumn of 1990 in Krajina, there were some high officials of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Babic testified here, he managed to mention three of them who were there at different points in time. How many can you enumerate, those who were in Krajina in 1990? And Krajina is also in Yugoslavia, in Croatia, in Europe, and so on and so forth. Citizens of Yugoslavia were, therefore, in Krajina. So how many of them were there there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that period that you are referring to, I know of one only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh. So one MUP high official in 1990 was in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the part that I know about. Perhaps there were more of them, but I know of one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then on the basis of that, that this one official, who perhaps may have been from that area originally, and as you know full well the one that we are mentioning does come from that area so he simply came to his native region. So does that provide for the statement that we heard here from the opposing side that the officials of the MUP of Serbia were staying in Krajina in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was staying in Dubrovnik in 1990, in 1991, in 1989. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It does not matter what the Prosecution said. You are referring to a statement, as you call it, from the other side. I take that to be a reference to the Prosecution. It's not for the witness to answer questions about what they said. All he can give evidence about is what he himself saw or heard, or indeed his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then as far as your personal knowledge is concerned, you are not contesting anything. You just know of one person who worked in the MUP of Serbia and who was in Krajina in 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is a high official of the MUP of Serbia, not any official. That is one thing. Secondly, he was not there on a private visit in Krajina and in Knin. He came with very specific assignments, and we had statements about that that we gathered towards the end of 1990 when we worked on documenting illegal armament both by the Serbs in Croatia too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not mention any names because that bothers you. This man, does he originally come from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of his origins. Judging by his name and surname, he may be from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then I can tell you that originally he does come from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Krajina. There is another thing that I'm going to challenge, but did you claim that Captain Dragan was a man of the DB, the state security, and that they brought him from Australia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the information that we received went, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You said that around Sid some paramilitary formations appeared and that no one knew who was sending them. Is that the way you put it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, specifically concerning the camp where training was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, did anybody send them or were they volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically I can mention a case that you are aware of, when Mr. Seselj had a rally, either at the square of the republic or by the trade unions building, and he was sending volunteers to the theatre of war. And this was on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you know full well that all opposition parties had many rallies, and I could not recall each and every rally, and I was not really all that interested either, but isn't it correct that all opposition parties had many rallies at that time? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not a problem. That is not an answer to what I said to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you the following now: Since you mentioned Dusan Silni, Mirko Jovic and then the Serb guard of the SPO and the Serb Radical Party, practically all major opposition parties set up some kind of volunteer detachments. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, they were trying to outdo each other in proving their Serbdom, and they were proud of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is this being challenged, that these were exclusively opposition parties in Serbia that were doing that at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I was talking about in that section of my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps the Socialist Party of Serbia, as the ruling party, did they set up some kind of volunteer units of their own or were all these detachments that you referred to established by various opposition parties?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned what was said in the TV programme made by the BBC, The Death of Yugoslavia, where Mr. Seselj stated that he armed and sent his own volunteers on -- according to the assignment issued to him by Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, General, does that mean you are testifying here on the basis of having watched the BBC?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; on the basis of what I heard Mr. Seselj say publicly. And partly he talked about that when he showed up in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If we have time, I'm going to ask you what else you saw on the BBC, but this is what you said that you saw on the BBC. All right. Is it being contested that opposition parties set up these paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't be contested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so it's not being contested.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's not only them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean? Did the Socialist Party of Serbia perhaps establish some volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are reducing it to parties now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that opposition parties set up some kind of volunteer detachments.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in addition to that, the people from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah, we're getting to that now, but just let me ask you one thing: Is it being contested that these opposition parties, precisely those that established these units, tried to topple me and the existing regime in Serbia on the 9th of March, 1991, and throughout the period of ten years, is that being contested? But let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Wait a moment. You've asked a question. Let the witness answer. You are being asked, General, about the 9th of March, 1991, a specific question. Can you answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I can answer that in Serbia, going from one party to another, the attitude of these parties varied towards the president. There was a right -- there was a right wing position that was taken and then there were others who went into coalitions with the SPS, the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go further on. If these opposition parties that established these detachments were organised -- I mean, these detachments were organised by the police, and you claim that I controlled the police, if that is correct, then the police worked against me. And if the police did not work against me, then what you have been saying cannot be true. Is that right or is that not right, General?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the police organised paramilitary formations of opposition parties that were working against the existing government, the existing president, and so on, the police of that same existing government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer that to clarify it, and then we'll adjourn. Yes, General. Can you answer that question or would you wish the accused to clarify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear. First of all, I did not claim that these paramilitary groups of the parties were organised by the people from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so you are not claiming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let the witness finish. It's impossible if you keep interrupting. Now, continue, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, but it was my understanding that that was his assertion. If that's not his assertion, then he can finish straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here's my answer: Even where they knew about this, they did not take measures according to the law. They tolerated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can I ask you something? Do you know how many extremists, Muslim extremists from the territory of Serbia, from Sandzak fought as volunteers in the army of Alija Izetbegovic? Was it a large number?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now going off on a totally different tangent. A totally different tangent, and we're going to adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I put a question to you: Do you know how many volunteers, Muslim extremists from Sandzak went to fight in the army of Alija Izetbegovic? That means from Serbia. And your answer was that you do not know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it your job, since you headed the security administration of the JNA, to know about things like that precisely?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is precisely what the state security of Serbia was supposed to be doing, because these are citizens of the Republic of Serbia. They are not military personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, if the state security did not prevent those extremists from going to fight in Alija Izetbegovic's army, can you infer on that basis that the state security sent them to fight there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why do you infer that the state security sent these volunteer units of these opposition parties that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they sent them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say, that they didn't prevent them from doing that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they could have prevented them had they had some information about that, and they did have some knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they not prevent these people from going from Sandzak? According to the same logic, they should have had that kind of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had that kind of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are resorted to inverted logic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, never mind. You said that you had information about a high official in Krajina who came from the MUP. Does that mean that you as the JNA security administration processed this official and that's how you had this information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had we processed him, we would have had a lot more information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have operative information or do you not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is this operative information that he was staying in Krajina and that he had a pseudonym, that he introduced himself as being someone else rather than who he was, and that, in contact with Martic, he was involved in the organisation of Serbs, volunteers, who later entered the camp in Golubici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since you had this particular information about one official of the police from Serbia who is a citizen of Yugoslavia and, therefore, he was staying in the territory of Yugoslavia, and you find that to be suspicious, did you have any information about some representatives of the police or similar services of foreign countries who were in the area at that time or around that time, if you had this particular piece of information about this one official from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you are obfuscating the issue. I can talk about that information as well. I can talk about paramilitary formations and what the MUP of Croatia was doing precisely in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, all right. The MUP of Croatia. But some other foreign countries, did you have information about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the region of Krajina, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the area of Croatia? Did you have that kind of information for Croatia as a whole?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one case around Opatovac, I believe, where bodies were found with IDs coming from foreign countries. But you should know at least that the security service of the JNA was not an almighty service controlling every single person. They had their own line of work and something that would come in as information that came in along with other kinds of information was also forwarded further on, but it was not our task to follow everything that was going on in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But if you claim that the security service of the army of Yugoslavia was not almighty, and of course I respect that, doesn't the same thing go to -- for the state security service, that they were not almighty either?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about them being almighty in the sense of that they cannot obtain information. I am trying to say that they are not supposed to compile information that does not fall within their own line of work. Also, the state security cannot know what the situation is in the army because they are not in charge. However, they are in charge of and responsible for knowing what the situation is amongst the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As much as possible.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have we clarified this, then, that it is not correct that the police of Serbia stood behind these paramilitary formations that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which formations specifically?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned Dusan Silni, Mirko Jovic, SPO, SRS, practically all of them opposition parties.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we can discuss this individually. I have no information that the state security service was behind the Dusan Silni detachment. However, the fact remains that this detachment from the territory of Serbia came there. And there is also the fact that two days after having given this information about the crime in Lovas to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, that I forwarded this information to the MUP of Serbia as well, believing that they are in charge of these persons who, from the territory of Serbia, came practically to the territory of Croatia. I am not aware of any reaction of theirs in spite of the fact that a crime had been committed. I gave information about specifically 12 persons whom we had identified, and one of them was a Greek, judging by his last name. So I think that everything is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely what is not clear, because you say that the police of Serbia, according to what you've said, were supposed to operate in the territory of Croatia in order to throw light on a crime that was committed in Croatia. Wasn't that within the powers of the army under whose control that area was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as the army is concerned, the military prosecutor was informed from the following aspect; that two military persons, the commander and the deputy commander of the detachment from Valjevo, partly participated in this event. However, the security service and the MUP of Serbia received information about 12 persons from that detachment who actually forced the Croats to be a human shield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you come to know that the police of Serbia did not do anything about persons who were citizens of Serbia who had committed some crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. Don't put words in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you know that as early as the beginning of 1993 persons were tried in Serbia for having committed crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina because it was established that they were our citizens?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I only know of the case of the Yellow Wasps, Zuta Osa, and I think that this trial was held in Loznica. I don't know about any other cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know that measures were taken against perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see now in Belgrade, it is only now that some persons are standing trial, and these were persons that were brought into custody before by the MUP of Serbia and then they were sent off to Republika Srpska because it was said that they were under their jurisdiction and that's where they were actually set free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the responsibility of Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now these very same persons are being tried in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is your explanation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what I've said is quite clear, that at that time that was tolerated. A modus operandi had been found. When somebody was supposed to be brought to justice, then they would be extradited and handed over, allegedly, to another area where they were supposed to be accountable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, and they were citizens of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this information, but I wish you'd give it to me.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. Specifically I know about Lukic. He is a citizen of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lukic who?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group that took part in liquidations around Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that a citizen of Republika Srpska, rather, Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've heard of the name, but as far as I know, this is a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, Republika Srpska. You mentioned a unit, or perhaps I didn't write it down properly, a unit called Crnogorac. Is that the way you put it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you do not know who was in that unit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know who commanded the unit?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who commanded the unit? I mean, if this is something that does not jeopardise your safety and security, please give an answer. So you don't have to answer anything that would jeopardise you in any way.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I mentioned that name in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not mention any names then. Did he go there as a volunteer or did somebody send him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know about that. All right. You said that as for the presence of some officials, Colonel Petrovic informed you about that, and he was a security organ somewhere there in Eastern Slavonia; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Petkovic, not Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, Petkovic, then.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there were other officers too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that some officials of the MUP came to the area of Sid to visit General Arandjelovic or Andjelkovic, commander of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. division; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Arandjelovic, commander of the division.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that this Colonel Petkovic of yours was sent away from these meetings.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that he would come to meetings with them and then the commander would send him away or did they simply come to pay a visit to the commander of the division and talk to him, ask him about the situation, collect information, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He saw them coming to see the commander, and he wanted to be present but then he was told that there was no need for him to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that they weren't discussing security issues. Perhaps they had come privately.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why they would keep coming on a private basis to visit the most responsible commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, tell me this, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was all covered in private session. I don't know whether the witness has given thought to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, if you want to go into private session, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as we've started talking about this particular area and if he's going to continue along those lines, we can stay in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we established the fact that your security organ, that is to say Colonel Petkovic, did not attend those talks but that he informed you as to the content of those talks. So how could he inform you if he didn't attend the talks themselves?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't put words into my mouth and say things I didn't state. I didn't say that he informed me as to the discussions that had been held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what they talked about.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Take it slowly. I want to explain what I mean. It was unnatural that the organs of internal affairs should come to visit the commanders, and they were probably coming officially, paying official visits. And it wasn't natural -- just a moment, please -- that a security organ was not present, because if the problems -- problems of security were being discussed, then they would be the competent organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use the word a moment ago "probably officially"? What if they hadn't come officially? You assumed they come officially and you say probably. That is your assumption.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say probably officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did use the word "probably officially."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was probably officially, but did they come privately? You know why they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't even know that they went. But you were explaining, let's take another example, that in 1989, as early on as then, while you were the division commander in Sarajevo, when you would go to visit a general, one of your colleagues who held a higher rank, you came across there somebody who was a later high official of the state security. So do you assume that they knew each other on a private basis and liked to have a chat and visit each other?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command and headquarters is not a place where you go to see someone privately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that nobody ever visited you privately at your workplace?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the security administration, if I did have a private visit, then it did not take place in my office; I had to go to the room for visitors. When I was a general as well, that applied then too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about the General Staff, are you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other commands as well. The rules are the same; the room for visitors is where you go for private visits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the commander of an army, for example, if somebody's coming to see him privately, is not allowed to receive that private visitor in his working office but has to go to the visitor's room; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, commanders can do anything they like, but I'm talking about rules and regulations. And here, quite obviously, these were not official visits and that it was building up relationships which would later come to their finale. The final act would come later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is your assumption, that somebody in 1989 was in fact building up relations with somebody -- or, rather, the state security was building up relations with someone in the army in 1989, and you exclude any private friendships, socialising on a private basis, and things of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have said enough on that subject, and the people who are called upon to draw their own conclusions will be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, those conclusions are not that deep that they cannot be drawn. I'm not quite sure whether this next question was discussed in private session. I haven't noted that down, but let me just mention what I'm talking about. The 28th of June, 1992, when General Panic issued an order of some kind. Was that discussed in private session? You were asked. That was the question that you were asked.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that, the 28th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question is, as I have noted it down, the following: That the commander of the Territorial Defence, Panic, ordered -- so Panic, who was in command in that area. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't the 28th of June, it was the 28th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then I read it out wrongly. Yes, I noted down the 28th of January. Did we discuss that in private session?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can talk about it in open session too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In open session too. Right. So he asked the commander of the Territorial Defence that Arkan's unit be sent away from the territory, from that area, and somebody told you, you said, that Radovan Stojicic at that time said that there wouldn't be any problems on that score because it would be within the frameworks of a brigade to be established by the MUP of Serbia. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention the commander of the Territorial Defence. You probably misspoke on that score. But an order did come out to disband and disarm the paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that order was quite in order; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of December. Of the Presidency. And according to that order, these formations and units were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were to be disbanded?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they hadn't been disbanded yet, and then General Panic issued an order to General Petkovic to come into contact with Stojicic and to caution him about that, and I said what he answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you say that Stojicic on that occasion said there'd be no problems because they'd come under the formation of the guards formed by the MUP of Serbia. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did the MUP of Serbia actually form a brigade in Eastern Slavonia? Do you happen to know that there was any kind of MUP of Serbia brigade in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm just saying what this man answered, not what he did subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You're telling us what somebody told you he had been told and not what he had answered.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That wasn't any wives' tale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about a material fact. To the best of your knowledge, was any kind of brigade of the MUP of Serbia formed on the territory of Eastern Slavonia? That's my question, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to go back and remember as to whether I received information of that kind, but I did have information that it was in a unit of this kind, in a brigade of this kind, that some of the people from the formations I mentioned earlier on did form part of that new formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, don't you find something illogical there? Was it not a question of the formation of units which was affected by the authorities of Krajina in the area? I don't know that any Serbian MUP Brigade existed in the area. Do you know about that? Do you have knowledge about its existence? That's what I'm asking you; was there, to your knowledge, a brigade by the MUP of Serbia established in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that question contains something I would like to ask you: Why did General Zivota Panic tell Colonel Petkovic that for Arkan's units he was to caution Stojicic Badza that they should be disbanded? What would have to do with that? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what you said was that part of those people or some of those people were citizens of Serbia, and therefore, he was drawing attention to the fact that citizens of Serbia, volunteers who had come there, should be sent away from the area. So what other explanation could you have? That's the logical explanation. Do you have a different explanation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell us then.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explanation is that Arkan's units at that time was under the absolute control of the people from the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you base that assertion? What do you base that assertion on that Arkan's volunteer guards were under the control of the MUP of Serbia? I'm hearing that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And did you hear that they had official identification cards of the state security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I heard that Arkan had an ID card issued by the federal MUP and state security or, rather, the Federal Secretariat for the Interior at the time the secretariat was headed by Stane Dolanc. He was the federal secretary of the day. That's what I heard, and I'm sure you know all about that better than me.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those identification cards were changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were changed but is what I'm telling you correct, this piece of information, that he did have documents issued by the federal SUP to him during the SFRY when Stane Dolanc, a Slovene, a leading Slovenian politician, was at the head of the state secretariat?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was at that early period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We, let's leave behind that farce about Arkan and the MUP of Serbia if it's quite clear that it was the federal SUP from the one time Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't put words into my mouth, please, and say things I didn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, and you can decide for yourself whether this jeopardises your safety and whether we need to go into private session to discuss it further, the meeting on the 25th of February, 1992, in Vukovar, where you said -- you told us the people who attended the meeting, and you said that they decided to place a commander for the Territorial Defence in Vukovar. Do you need a private session?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we don't name names, I don't need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. May I quote one name which is not a threat to you? And the name is Goran Hadzic, who was at that time the president of Eastern Slavonia, the president of the Assembly, or the Prime Minister, whichever you like, of the autonomous province of Eastern Slavonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it under his competence and authority to appoint a commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what came under his competence and authority, if you were to read the rules and regulations and laws you read out to begin with, then it would appear that this was some sort of improvisation following along from that. However, it is not the aim of my discussion to address those issues but that two men from the MUP of Serbia were appointed to be the commander and the Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, then: Those two men for whom you say were from the MUP of Serbia, I don't know, I don't know the names so I can't say for sure myself, but were they, at the time, working in the MUP of Serbia or had they come as volunteers because they originated from the area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite understand how an active duty officer can become a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not, if he leaves his work post and goes off somewhere to be a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would have had to leave his work post first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know he didn't?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I said the two men came from the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't work in the MUP of Serbia and be in the Territorial Defence over there. That's impossible. They might have had some job to do in the MUP of Serbia and weren't able to continue doing that job if they went over there.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I said was that they were from the MUP of Serbia and were appointed to that post; and second, that Badza Stojicic was also an official of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when he did that he wasn't an official of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who could he carry on his work and function in the MUP of Serbia if he was over there on a volunteer basis to help with the defence in Eastern Slavonia, for example?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would have to go into private session if you want me to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a logical question. It doesn't call for a private session at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness feels more comfortable in a private session, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that somebody had been appointed, quite obviously by the competent organs over there, to head the Territorial Defence, and you also said at the same time and parallelly speaking about other matters, that active officers were appointed at the head of TO Krajina, active officials of the JNA, officers of the JNA. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sent to take up posts in the Ministry of Defence of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Active officers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were active, and on the basis of procedure, they were sent there. Before that, they had been active officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does that confirm that the Territorial Defence was under the control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Right. I have something to ask you now related to the financing that you talked about. You said that Yugoslavia, the army of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslavia financed or gave financial assistance to the army of Republika Srpska and the army of Srpska Krajina from Serbia, and it is not disputed that it did give financial assistance. So please tell me this: Answer a very simple question now, please. Did the army of Yugoslavia -- because you linked this up, did it have any functions with respect to issuing orders to combat activity of the army of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina? Did it do that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge about that because I was outside active duty service at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, is it clear that these were separate armies, separate institutions, separate states, and from this materially it has to be separated because it is not in dispute? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would one army send requests to another army to send soldiers who dodged the call-up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why was there correspondence addressed by one army to another army, asking officers to be sent to them which refused to respond to the call-up if these were two separate armies in absolute terms?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, is it clear that while the SFRY still existed, these were all officers of one and the same army called the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear speak about the meeting between Branko Kostic and Veljko Kadijevic and Alija Izetbegovic when they agreed that members of the JNA originating from Bosnia-Herzegovina should return to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you mention that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But it wasn't General Kadijevic but Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm sorry. I made a mistake. So Branko Kostic, the vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, and Blagoje Adzic, when he had replaced Kadijevic, anyway the number one man, number one general in the army, had a meeting with Alija Izetbegovic at which Izetbegovic requested that members of the JNA originating from Bosnia-Herzegovina should all return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that they should leave the JNA and come to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was implying the Bosniaks in the first place, but he also requested that citizens who are not from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and are members of the JNA should leave Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And did the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, when it was formed on the 28th of April, 1992, withdrew all citizens born in Serbia and Montenegro - that is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little later. There was some delay, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the dynamics was determined by logistic and technical problems but certainly not by any hesitation to do that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it strange then if the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina ask -- make the same request as Izetbegovic made from Hadzic and Kostic to allow officers coming from their area, born there, to return and join the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were active-duty officers of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when we were talking about Izetbegovic, they were also active officers.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm not talking about Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I am. Wasn't he referring to active duty officers to return?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it in this case too those who wanted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who wanted could remain in the army of Yugoslavia. But contrary to their wish, another army was asked to extradite them, to put it very crudely, to an army in another state, and this was a request made to the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a very clear-cut piece of information in that connection, but let us clear this up first: Did anyone among the citizens of Krajina or Republika Srpska, was anyone sent by force to the army of Republika Srpska and the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina by the JNA, or were they officers from that area who wanted to go there and assist in the defence of those areas?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that they were taken there by force, but I do know that those who didn't want to go suffered certain consequences with respect to the status they enjoyed at the time, and I mentioned examples, the example of a Macedonian who happened to be born in Sarajevo, and on whom pressure was brought to bear that he would have to go to Sarajevo again to join the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a problem in the army and that is meaningless, just by the place of birth. It has nothing to do with that. It was just a bureaucratic problem.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and you intervened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I hadn't intervened, it would have probably been solved differently. But didn't you say a moment ago that no one was forced to join the army of Republika Srpska or the Republic of Serbian Krajina even though they were citizens of those republics and not of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I said something else which you're not mentioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there was a pressure on them with regard to the status they had in the service. I might also add that all those persons didn't have the usual ID of a citizen of Yugoslavia but, rather, they had a marking on their ID with the letter "T" or "Transit," meaning that they had served in the army of Yugoslavia, and for many years they could not acquire Yugoslav citizenship. So this process of granting citizenship to members of the army of Yugoslavia was accelerated only after the changes of the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which members of the army of Yugoslavia? Who were from that other region?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They couldn't get citizenship for years. It was not possible to resolve their status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were officers of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were officers. And they submitted a request to that effect, but for years this was tabled in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know very well that the question of citizenship was resolved in the Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs and not the MUP of Serbia. You should be familiar with those regulations. Yes, but let me ask you, is this true -- in view of your testimony, I have here a completely different information or version, so please would you comment on it and tell me whether it is correct or not. "All officers who, as volunteers, went to Krajina and Bosnia were called up as a result of requests from Krajina and the Republika Srpska." Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm afraid I'm unable to give you a clear-cut answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But if we're talking about active-duty officers of the JNA, and they were called up and this question was raised in the JNA, you, for instance, are from Krajina, and you are asked by the leadership of Krajina to assist them in the defence, you're an active-duty officer of the JNA, and you have to raise the issue with your superiors in your unit; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Allow me to answer. I did respond to such questions by saying that he could go there, but that he should first be demobilised from the JNA, that he should terminate his service in the JNA, after which he can go where he wants to. That's what happened. You're probably referring to the army of Yugoslavia, but you mentioned the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I meant the army of Yugoslavia. Discussions were organised with those officers, or interviews, who at the request of people from Krajina or from Republika Srpska were required to go back there, and at those meetings, they would state whether they want to go to their native area or not. And here is the information I have: At those meetings, about 80 per cent of those who were requested to go back there refused to go. I don't know whether this figure is accurate. I thought until now that if a larger number accepted to go -- but those who refused to go, no one sent there on the part of the army of Yugoslavia because they had no right to do so in view of the fact that there was fighting in another state. Therefore, those who refused to go were not ordered to go, either to Bosnia or to Krajina. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that meetings were held with those officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they discussed with them whether they wanted to go or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is also true that those discussions did have the effect of a certain psychological pressure. This was just not mere voluntariness. I would not have been asked in one particular case to intervene so that that officer would not go there. So I think if it had been absolute voluntariness, a man would say he didn't want to go and nothing would happen. As far as I know, there were two distinct periods, the period of 1993, when there was clear pressure brought on such officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the part of whom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the part of officers in responsible positions, that he had to go to serve in Bijeljina. I have the specific case of one of my deputies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Bijeljina. Either he would be pensioned off or he would go to Bijeljina. And I had to intervene to keep him in active service. This was in 1993. In 1992 -- that is the second half of 1992 and the beginning of 1993. Later on, this was -- the pressure was reduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the second half of 1992 and beginning of 1993, weren't you already retired?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking to you globally about this period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you're saying second half of 1992 and 1993. You were a pensioner at the time. What assistant are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to answer your question. I cannot give you an answer if you keep interrupting me. So this particular case I'm talking about happened in April 1992, the specific example I'm mentioning, when a man had to retire or go over there. But I'm speaking about the situation globally, from mid-1992 to 1993. I can tell you who was pensioned off in that period and why the climate afterwards changed. You mentioned the meetings that were held when people were persuaded to go. That's a different situation in relation to 1992 and 1993. And this was also used for a kind of ethnic cleansing of the army of those who were not born in Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you talking about? Cleansing from Serbs who were not born in Serbia, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just that. Let me tell you that I was asked by a high-ranking general to remove from service all those who were not Serbs and Montenegrins, and even a Croat who had been discovered, a very important case in Croatia that is public knowledge, and I refused to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you were quite right in doing that, but do you know, General, that that never was the policy of Yugoslavia nor the policy of the political leadership of Yugoslavia or Serbia, to remove anyone on the basis of their ethnicity from the army of Yugoslavia? After all, in 1999, your immediate superior, the chief of the security administration in the army of Yugoslavia, was a Hungarian. And there were generals who were Muslims and Albanians and people of all ethnicities in the army of Yugoslavia. Only in Serbia and Montenegro. And in Serbia, while I was the president, no one was discriminated against on the basis of ethnicity. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you an answer. First of all, when we spoke on the 5th of March, 1992, about why my deputy had been replaced, General Tumanov, who was a Macedonian, you literally gave me the following answer: "When in the Macedonian army they appoint a Serb as deputy chief of their service, security service, then we will appoint Tumanov here for the chief." So that is one example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Tumanov wasn't replaced then for that reason.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going into the reasons for his replacement. But that's out of the question. There were questions given to us as to whether we were married to Muslims, and you received such information even in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not true, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am saying is true. And secondly, when you're talking about Geza, there's no dispute that he's Hungarian, a citizen of Yugoslavia, though. I don't know whether you know that when your Minister of Internal Affairs, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, came to see General Ojdanic for a meeting and asked whether General Ojdanic was alone, when his adjutant said that Geza was inside - I feel embarrassed in saying this but I have to say it - he said, "Are you still keeping that Hungarian here?" If I'm embarrassed to say that, I've still decided to say it, I'm not making it up. I'm talking about the climate that was in evidence. There is no dispute that there were generals who were Albanian and those who were Hungarian and Muslim. There's no dispute over that. But I do know that many other honourable men, among them numerous pilots, Slovenes, Croats, who did something that maybe a Serb would not have done in those days also had to leave their positions. That is how the commander of the air force was removed and all others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which commander of the air force was removed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvonko Jurjevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you perhaps follow when I showed a tape here or played a tape of a conversation between Kadijevic and Tudjman after the signing of the cease-fire in Igalo, in the presence of Lord Carrington, when Tudjman says to Kadijevic, "Very well, even Jurjevic has not returned to you," and Kadijevic tells him, "I know why he didn't return. It's up to him." So he wasn't replaced, but he stayed on when he went to Zagreb for a weekend and never returned. So he said it's to his credit. Why are you saying that when it's not true, when we have material fact that he abandoned the service?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Let the witness deal with the conversation which was alleged to have been on the tape. Can you help us at all about that particular case, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. So you've made a mistake. It is not Zvonko Jurjevic, it is probably General Tus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tus went before him and he became the Chief of General Staff in Croatia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish. Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jurjevic was retired. I believe on the 8th or 9th of February, 1992. He still lives in Belgrade. He hasn't gone anywhere. And he was persecuted. I know that. I know that personally. He was chased with a knife and with a pistol in the streets of Belgrade because he was proclaimed to be a traitor. And he's a greater Yugoslav than I am. Let me tell you one more thing. As far as Tus is concerned, he did not escape or run away. He was pensioned off according to normal procedure, and he went to live where his family was, namely in Zagreb. So he did not desert the JNA. He was pensioned off, and he went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was he pensioned off?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was pensioned off in June 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is that at the time when you yourself say that I did not have any influence on the top military leadership?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the top military leadership that I was in, these are the closest --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there's one top military leadership, not a hundred of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time, please. Let the witness finish. Don't interrupt his train of thought. You were dealing with the top military leadership, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a rather indefinite term. Who are actually the generals in the top military leadership? I consider as the top military leadership the federal secretary, the Chief of General Staff, and their closest associates who make up the top staff of the federal secretary. And there are other high-ranking generals who were in the General Staff, but they did not belong to what I call the top military leadership. To the best of my knowledge, in that stage you did not have considerable influence over that top military leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not have any influence.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that there were some generals, and I gave examples of who you directly talked to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did I talk to directly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in closed session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is not under wraps in any way. Who was it that I talked to, and why do you infer on that basis that I have influence over the military leadership?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just saying now that it is unusual for the president of a republic, any republic, to communicate without the knowledge of his superior of any -- with any general, and that is what you did then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, wait a minute. I don't see that this is a question for a closed session. I hope you will agree with that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. What is it that we should discuss?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. You say that I spoke on the telephone with Zivota Panic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zivota Panic commander of the 1st Army then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was deputy Chief of General Staff for the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. For the ground forces. So at any rate, he was in charge of the ground forces. Do you know, first of all, as for General Panic, I knew him only superficially. I had only a few contacts with him. Do you know that at that time when I was looking for him I actually answered his telephone call because they connected me because he had called me before that. And do you know why he called me? Now, that is again a question that has to do again with your own internal procedure, not mine, because I am a well-brought up person and I respond to calls that are made to me. He called me because the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, paragraphs 118 and 119 -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraphs 118 and 119, the witness may be really being pushed into a position of going into open session where he has little chance but to agree to the accused's proposals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go into private session then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that I'll be given Monday and Tuesday of next week for my examination of this witness, because I started my cross-examination in the latter half of today. So could you please tell me. I don't want to get any surprises and shortenings which would upset my cross-examination, so could you tell me now how much time. He began the week before last to testify, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let us work that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On a rough calculation, it seems you've got 7 hours, 45 minutes. But that's a rough calculation. So that, I think, will take care of tomorrow and Monday. But work on that basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But that would then be less than two and a half days, Mr. May, whereas he testified for three days. Tomorrow is the second day, Monday the third day, and examination-in-chief took longer than three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've worked it out on an hourly basis, not on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, work it out on an hourly basis, it comes to the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the ruling for the moment. We will adjourn and sit again tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
